implementation_notes: The std answer and the default: a static OnceLock<T> starts empty, get_or_init runs the builder on first call with the synchronisation and memory ordering handled by std, and every caller then receives an immutable &T. The classic structure disappears together with its hazard - the borrow checker only hands out a reference to a fully initialised value, so a partially published object is unrepresentable rather than merely unlikely.
pitfalls: A check-then-initialise accessor built on get() (or on a lock-guarded Option) is still the race the pattern is about: get() returns None while another thread initialises, so two builders run and the loser's value is dropped.
OnceLock is one-shot and cannot be reset - take() needs &mut self - so reloading needs RwLock<Option<T>> or an ArcSwap, and a failed build cannot be retried through the same cell.
The cell hands out &T only, so post-initialisation mutability must live inside the value (Mutex/RwLock/atomic) and types needing interior mutability pay for it.
Initialisation happens on the first caller's thread: a slow or panicking builder blocks every other caller (and a panic inside get_or_init leaves the cell unset, so the next caller retries).

variants.name: LazyLock for static values built by a closure
variants.implementation_notes: LazyLock (Rust 1.80) is OnceLock plus the closure: the deref of the static runs the builder on first use, which keeps the declaration to one line and removes the accessor function entirely. Prefer it for configuration-like statics that are read directly; prefer OnceLock when the value needs arguments known only at run time or when the initialisation must be fallible.
pitfalls: Deref-ing the static from inside its own initialiser deadlocks (the guard is non-reentrant), so LazyLock must not be used to break a cyclic dependency between statics.
The initialiser cannot fail: a fallible build needs OnceLock plus a Result payload (or a panic, which poisons nothing here but aborts the work).
Lazy statics hidden behind Deref make start-up work appear at an arbitrary first use, which is harder to trace than an explicit initialisation point.

variants.name: Once::call_once with a manually managed cell
variants.implementation_notes: The low-level form, stable since Rust 1.0 and still the only one when the initialised state is not a single owned value (several interdependent statics, or side-effecting setup such as installing a panic hook). The data itself must then be managed by hand - a static mut behind unsafe, or a wrapper - which is exactly the unsafe code that OnceLock exists to remove; use it for side effects, not for values.
pitfalls: The unsafe cell is only sound because call_once establishes the happens-before edge: reading it outside a call_once/wait pair, or writing it elsewhere, is undefined behaviour.
A panic inside call_once poisons the Once: every later call panics as well (call_once_force is the escape hatch), so panicking initialisers change the failure mode of the whole process.
Recursive call_once on the same Once is unspecified (panic or deadlock), which is the low-level analogue of the re-entrancy hazard in the classic pattern.
